charles-perry-food-writer.name: Charles Perry
charles-perry-food-writer.summary: American food historian, born 1941, who has translated medieval Arabic cookbooks into English and written widely on the history of food, especially the Middle East and California.

ubayd-zakani.name: Ubayd Zakani
ubayd-zakani.summary: Persian poet of the Mongol era (died 1370), regarded as one of the best satirists in Persian literature. His bawdy, provocative works were little studied by modern scholars until recently.

encyclop-dia-iranica.name: Encyclopædia Iranica
encyclop-dia-iranica.summary: Project aiming to create a comprehensive and authoritative English-language encyclopedia on the history, culture and civilization of Iranian peoples, from prehistory to modern times.

the-canon-of-medicine.name: The Canon of Medicine
the-canon-of-medicine.summary: Five-book medical encyclopedia completed by Ibn Sina (Avicenna) in 1025. Translated into Latin in 12th-century Toledo, it became a standard textbook in European universities into the early modern period.

zakhireye-khwarazmshahi.name: Zakhireye Khwarazmshahi
zakhireye-khwarazmshahi.summary: Persian medical encyclopedia written in 1110 by the physician Ismail Gorgani. Its title means 'Treasure Dedicated to the King of Khwarazm'.

zayn-al-din-gorgani.name: Zayn al-Din Gorgani
zayn-al-din-gorgani.summary: Persian court physician from Gorgan (about 1040 to 1136) who moved to Khwarazm in 1110. He dedicated his most influential work, a Persian medical compendium, to the Khwarazm-Shah Qutb al-Din Muhammad I.

ilkhanate.name: Ilkhanate
ilkhanate.summary: A Mongol khanate established by Hülegü, grandson of Genghis Khan, ruling Iran and neighboring lands from 1259; it converted to Islam under Ghazan and collapsed after ruler Abu Sa'id died in 1335.

timurid-empire.name: Timurid Empire
timurid-empire.summary: A Turco-Mongol, Persian-influenced Muslim empire founded by Timur in 1370, dominating Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan and Central Asia into the 15th century.

genghis-khan.name: Genghis Khan
genghis-khan.summary: Founder of the Mongol Empire (c. 1162-1227), who united the Mongol tribes and conquered large parts of China and Central Asia.

merv.name: Merv
merv.summary: A major ancient Iranian city in Central Asia on the Silk Road, settled from the 3rd millennium BC, that at times served as capital of the caliphate and of the Great Seljuk Empire and became a center of Islamic science.

nishapur.name: Nishapur
nishapur.summary: A city in northeastern Iran, founded in the 3rd century by Shapur I, later capital of the Tahirid dynasty and initial capital of the Seljuk Empire.

ray-iran.name: Ray (Rayy)
ray-iran.summary: An ancient city in Iran, now part of Greater Tehran; a prominent city of Media in classical times, later revived as a capital under the Buyid and Seljuk dynasties.

isfahan.name: Isfahan
isfahan.summary: City in central Iran that flourished from the 9th to 18th centuries and became the Safavid capital under Abbas the Great, renowned for its Persian-Muslim architecture.

timurid-architecture.name: Timurid architecture
timurid-architecture.summary: A grand architectural style of palaces, mausoleums and mosques across Iran and Central Asia under the Timurid dynasty (1370–1507), known for elaborate tilework and vaulting.

gawhar-shad.name: Gawhar Shad
gawhar-shad.summary: The chief consort of Shah Rukh, emperor of the Timurid Empire; she died in 1457.

shah-rukh.name: Shah Rukh
shah-rukh.summary: Son of Timur (Tamerlane) who ruled the eastern Timurid Empire from 1405 to 1447, controlling Silk Road trade and making Herat his capital and a centre of art and science.

mashhad.name: Mashhad
mashhad.summary: The second-largest city in Iran, home to the Imam Reza Shrine, one of the holiest sites in Shia Islam and among the most pilgrimaged sites in the world.

herat.name: Herat
herat.summary: Ancient city in western Afghanistan on the Silk Road that became a major center of the Timurid Renaissance after being conquered by Timur.

yuan-dynasty.name: Yuan dynasty
yuan-dynasty.summary: A Mongol-led dynasty ruling China from 1271 to 1368, founded by Kublai Khan, and the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China.

seljuk-empire.name: Seljuk Empire
seljuk-empire.summary: A medieval Turco-Persian empire founded in 1037 by brothers Tughril and Chaghri, stretching from Anatolia to Central Asia, whose 1071 victory at Manzikert weakened Byzantine control there.

kharraqan-towers.name: Kharraqan Towers
kharraqan-towers.summary: A pair of octagonal brick mausoleums built in 1067 and 1093 CE near Qazvin, Iran, notable as early examples of geometric ornament and double-dome design from the Seljuk era.

qazvin.name: Qazvin
qazvin.summary: A city in northwestern Iran that served as capital of the Safavid Empire from 1555 to 1598 and is known today as Iran's calligraphy capital.

bukhara.name: Bukhara
bukhara.summary: Ancient Silk Road city in what is now Uzbekistan, a major center of Islamic scholarship and birthplace of Imam Bukhari, later capital of the Emirate of Bukhara until 1920.

samarkand.name: Samarkand
samarkand.summary: A major city in southeastern Uzbekistan and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Central Asia, a key Silk Road center once capital of the Achaemenid satrapy of Sogdiana.

tus-iran.name: Tus
tus-iran.summary: An ancient city in Khorasan near modern Mashhad, Iran, known to the ancient Greeks as Susia.

ghaznavid-empire.name: Ghaznavid Empire
ghaznavid-empire.summary: Persianate Muslim empire of Turkic origin that flourished from 977 to 1186, stretching at its height from the Oxus River to the Indus Valley.

mahmud-of-ghazni.name: Mahmud of Ghazni
mahmud-of-ghazni.summary: Sultan of the Ghaznavid Empire from 998 to 1030 whose campaigns extended his rule from Iran to the Punjab, laying the foundation for Muslim rule in the Indian subcontinent.

ali-tegin.name: Ali-Tegin
ali-tegin.summary: Karakhanid ruler in Transoxiana from 1020 to 1034, with a brief interruption in 1024/25.

khorasan.name: Khorasan
khorasan.summary: A historical region of the Iranian Plateau spanning parts of modern Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia, with boundaries that varied over time and roots reaching back to Bronze Age complex societies there.

anushtegin-dynasty.name: Anushtegin dynasty
anushtegin-dynasty.summary: A Sunni Turkic Muslim dynasty of mamluk origin that ruled the Khwarazmian Empire across Central Asia, Afghanistan and Iran from about 1077 until the Mongol conquest in the 13th century.

battle-of-dandanaqan.name: Battle of Dandanaqan
battle-of-dandanaqan.summary: An 1040 battle near Merv in which Seljuq Turkmen forces decisively defeated the Ghaznavid Empire, ending Ghaznavid rule over Greater Khorasan.

kara-khanid-khanate.name: Kara-Khanid Khanate
kara-khanid-khanate.summary: A Karluk Turkic khanate that ruled Central Asia from the 9th to early 13th century, shifting the region from Iranic to Turkic dominance while adopting Perso-Arab Muslim culture.

battle-of-ghazni-1117.name: Battle of Ghazni
battle-of-ghazni-1117.summary: An 1117 battle between Seljuk forces backing Bahram of Ghazna and the army of his brother, the ruling Sultan Arslan-Shah of Ghazna.

transoxiana.name: Transoxiana
transoxiana.summary: A Central Asian region beyond the Amu Darya river, named by Alexander the Great's troops in the 4th century BCE and later a Persian Achaemenid province called Sogdia.

ahmad-sanjar.name: Ahmad Sanjar
ahmad-sanjar.summary: Seljuq ruler of Khorasan from 1097 and Sultan of the Seljuq Empire from 1118 until his death in 1157, whose long reign held the empire's borders together despite setbacks and his capture by Oghuz Turkmen in 1153.

ferdowsi.name: Ferdowsi
ferdowsi.summary: Persian poet (940–1025) who wrote the Shahnameh, one of the world's longest epic poems by a single author and one of the greatest works in Persian literature.

shahnameh.name: Shahnameh
shahnameh.summary: An epic poem of about 50,000 couplets written by the Persian poet Ferdowsi between around 977 and 1010 CE, telling Iran's mythical and historical past up to the Muslim conquest. It is regarded as Iran's national epic.

ruba-i.name: Ruba'i
ruba-i.summary: A four-line quatrain form in Persian poetry with a set rhyme scheme, used by poets including Rumi, Omar Khayyam and Mahsati Ganjavi.

omar-khayyam.name: Omar Khayyam
omar-khayyam.summary: Persian polymath (1048–1131) who advanced mathematics and astronomy, designed the precise Jalali solar calendar, and is traditionally credited with quatrain poetry.

mahsati.name: Mahsati Ganjavi
mahsati.summary: Medieval Persian poet reportedly among the first to compose ruba'iyat (quatrains) in her native language.

rumi.name: Rumi
rumi.summary: Sufi mystic and poet (1207–1273) who founded the Mevlevi Order; his Masnavi is considered one of the greatest works of Persian literature.

balkh.name: Balkh
balkh.summary: A city in northern Afghanistan, historically a center of Zoroastrianism and Buddhism known to Persians as Zariaspa and Greeks as Bactra; capital of ancient Bactria, later devastated by the Mongols.

konya.name: Konya (Iconium)
konya.summary: City in central Turkey known in antiquity as Iconium, later capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, and today the spiritual centre of the Whirling Dervishes.

khwaday-namag.name: Khwaday-Namag
khwaday-namag.summary: A lost Middle Persian 'Book of Lords/Kings' from the Sasanian era, recounting Iran's legendary history and believed to be a source for Ferdowsi's later Shahnameh.

rubaiyat-of-omar-khayyam.name: Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam
rubaiyat-of-omar-khayyam.summary: An 1859 English translation by Edward FitzGerald of quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam, which became hugely popular from the 1880s and inspired 'Omar Khayyam clubs.'

edward-fitzgerald-poet.name: Edward FitzGerald
edward-fitzgerald-poet.summary: An English poet and writer (1809-1883) whose 1859 translation of The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam remains the best-known English version, popular since the 1860s.

nizami-ganjavi.name: Nizami Ganjavi
nizami-ganjavi.summary: 12th-century Persian poet (c. 1141-1209), considered the greatest romantic epic poet in Persian literature, author of the Khamsa, which includes Layla and Majnun.

khamsa-of-nizami.name: Khamsa of Nizami
khamsa-of-nizami.summary: A collection of five long poems, also called the Panj Ganj or 'Five Treasures,' and the best-known work of the 12th-century Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi.

sanai.name: Sanai
sanai.summary: Iranian Sufi poet from Ghazni, best known for The Walled Garden of Truth, regarded as a pioneer of Persian Sufi poetry who influenced Attar and Rumi.

layla-and-majnun.name: Layla and Majnun
layla-and-majnun.summary: An ancient Arab love story about the 7th-century poet Qays ibn al-Mulawwah and his lover Layla, later retold across Arabic, Persian, Turkish and Indic literature.

jahan-malek-khatun.name: Jahan Malek Khatun
jahan-malek-khatun.summary: Injuid princess and 14th-century Persian poet who wrote under the pen name Jahan, a contemporary of the celebrated poet Hafez.

hafez.name: Hafez
hafez.summary: 14th-century Persian lyric poet (1325 to 1390) whose collected ghazals are regarded by many Iranians as a pinnacle of Persian literature and shaped later Persian writing more than any other author.

zend.name: Zend
zend.summary: A Zoroastrian term for Middle Persian translations and commentaries on Avestan scripture, produced in the late Sasanian period for religious instruction of believers who no longer spoke Avestan.

jalayirid-sultanate.name: Jalayirid Sultanate
jalayirid-sultanate.summary: A Mongol dynasty that ruled Iraq and western Iran after the Ilkhanate's breakup in the 1330s, lasting until eliminated by the Qara Qoyunlu in 1432; noted for patronizing Persian art.

aq-qoyunlu.name: Aq Qoyunlu
aq-qoyunlu.summary: A Turkoman, Persian-influenced Sunni Muslim tribal confederation that ruled eastern Turkey from 1378 and later Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Iraq, peaking under Uzun Hasan.

yaqub-aq-qoyunlu.name: Yaqub Beg
yaqub-aq-qoyunlu.summary: Ruler of the Aq Qoyunlu dynasty from 1478 until his death in 1490, praised by contemporaries for supporting poets and scientists.

ghazal.name: Ghazal
ghazal.summary: Poetic form originating in 7th-century Arabic poetry that deals with love and loss, later flourishing in Persian poetry and spreading across South Asia and Turkey.

sheema-kalbasi.name: Sheema Kalbasi
sheema-kalbasi.summary: An Iranian, Danish and American poet and filmmaker, born in 1972 in Tehran, whose work addresses feminism, war, refugees and human rights.

chagatai-language.name: Chagatai language
chagatai-language.summary: A now-extinct Turkic literary language once widely spoken across Central Asia until the early 20th century, and the direct ancestor of modern Uzbek and Uyghur.

karluks.name: Karluks
karluks.summary: A nomadic Turkic tribal confederacy of Central Asia active from about the 5th to 8th centuries CE; most Uzbeks and Uyghurs descend from them, and their languages form the Karluk subgroup of Turkic.

panemone-windmill.name: Panemone windmill
panemone-windmill.summary: A vertical-axis windmill design, the earliest known wind machine, made by the Persians using sail-covered slats around a vertical axle to grind grain or draw water.

al-biruni.name: Al-Biruni
al-biruni.summary: Iranian polymath of the Islamic Golden Age (c. 973-1050) who served the Ghaznavids as a historian and court astrologer and wrote a landmark work on India around 1030.

nandana.name: Nandana
nandana.summary: A ruined fortified settlement in Punjab, Pakistan, built by the Odi Shahi dynasty between 822 and 1026 CE.

avicenna.name: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
avicenna.summary: Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), known in the West as Avicenna, was a leading philosopher and physician of the Islamic Golden Age whose Canon of Medicine remained a standard European medical text until 1650.

mansur-ibn-ilyas.name: Mansur ibn Ilyas
mansur-ibn-ilyas.summary: A Persian physician from Shiraz active in the late 14th and early 15th centuries, known for producing Mansur's Anatomy, an early colored atlas of the human body.

ghazni.name: Ghazni
ghazni.summary: City in southeastern Afghanistan, historically the capital of the Ghaznavid Empire and today the capital of Ghazni Province.

ziyarid-dynasty.name: Ziyarid dynasty
ziyarid-dynasty.summary: An Iranian dynasty of Gilaki origin that ruled Tabaristan from 931 to 1090, reaching its height under Mardavij and later attracting scholars such as al-Biruni.

tabaristan.name: Tabaristan
tabaristan.summary: A mountainous region on Iran's Caspian coast, corresponding to today's Mazandaran province, which became the area's common name from the 11th century onward.

qabus.name: Qabus
qabus.summary: Ziyarid ruler of Gurgan and Tabaristan in medieval Iran, reigning 977–981 and 997–1012, who died in 1012.

mas-ud-i.name: Mas'ud I of Ghazni
mas-ud-i.summary: Sultan of the Ghaznavid Empire from 1030 to 1040, known as 'the martyr king', who seized the throne from his twin brother before being deposed by his own rebelling troops.

maragheh-observatory.name: Maragheh observatory
maragheh-observatory.summary: A 13th-century astronomical observatory in Persia, founded under the Ilkhanid ruler Hulagu and directed by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, considered one of the most advanced scientific institutions in Eurasia.

nasir-al-din-al-tusi.name: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi
nasir-al-din-al-tusi.summary: A Persian polymath (1201–1274) who advanced astronomy and trigonometry, created influential planetary tables, and is regarded as one of medieval Islam's greatest scientists.

hulegu-khan.name: Hulegu Khan
hulegu-khan.summary: Mongol ruler (c. 1217–1265) and grandson of Genghis Khan who conquered much of West Asia, founded the Ilkhanate in Persia, and destroyed Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid dynasty.

ma-munids.name: Ma'munids
ma-munids.summary: Short-lived dynasty of Iranian rulers in Khwarazm, 995 to 1017, later replaced by the expansionist Ghaznavids.

konye-urgench.name: Gurganj
konye-urgench.summary: Ancient city and former capital of Khwarazm, in what is now Konye-Urgench, Turkmenistan; abandoned in the early 18th century and now a UNESCO World Heritage ruin.

abu-nasr-mansur.name: Abu Nasr Mansur
abu-nasr-mansur.summary: Persian mathematician and astronomer (c. 960-1036), born to the ruling Afrighid family of Khwarezm, known for work on the spherical sine law and as al-Biruni's teacher and colleague.

tughril-i.name: Tughril
tughril-i.summary: Turkoman chieftain who founded the Seljuk Empire, ruling from 1037 to 1063 after uniting Turkoman tribes and conquering Persia and Baghdad.

chaghri-beg.name: Chaghri Beg
chaghri-beg.summary: Co-ruler of the early Seljuk Empire (989-1060), whose Turkic name means 'small falcon.'

hindu-kush.name: Hindu Kush
hindu-kush.summary: An 800-kilometre mountain range running from Afghanistan into Pakistan and Tajikistan, historically a center of Buddhism and a crossing point between Central and South Asia.

timur.name: Timur (Tamerlane)
timur.summary: Turco-Mongol conqueror (1320s–1405) who founded the Timurid Empire across Central Asia and the Middle East, seen as one of history's greatest and most brutal military leaders.

m-ngke-khan.name: Möngke Khan
m-ngke-khan.summary: The fourth khagan of the Mongol Empire, ruling 1251–1259, who oversaw conquests of Iraq, Syria and the Dali Kingdom; his death without a successor triggered a civil war that split the empire.

khwarazmian-empire.name: Khwarazmian Empire
khwarazmian-empire.summary: A Persianate, Turkic-founded Muslim empire ruling Central Asia, Afghanistan and Iran from 1077 to 1231, which grew from Seljuk vassal into the region's most powerful state before falling to the Mongols.

qara-khitai.name: Qara Khitai
qara-khitai.summary: A dynastic state founded in Central Asia by Khitans displaced after the fall of the Liao dynasty, governing a mostly Turkic and Iranian population until conquered by the Mongols in 1218.

atsiz.name: Ala al-Din Atsiz
atsiz.summary: Second Khwarazmshah, ruling from 1127 to 1156 as son and successor of Muhammad I.

khwarazm.name: Khwarazm
khwarazm.summary: A large oasis region on the Amu Darya river delta in Central Asia, center of the Iranian Khwarezmian civilization until Turkic tribes took over in the 9th century.

ghurid-dynasty.name: Ghurid dynasty
ghurid-dynasty.summary: A Persianate dynasty from the Ghor region of central Afghanistan that converted to Sunni Islam and grew into an empire from 1175 to 1215, overrunning the Ghaznavids.

ghazan.name: Ghazan
ghazan.summary: Seventh ruler of the Mongol Ilkhanate (r. 1295–1304), best known for converting to Islam in 1295 and reforming the empire's currency and fiscal policy.

al-qa-im.name: al-Qa'im
al-qa-im.summary: Abbasid caliph at Baghdad from 1031 to 1075, son of al-Qadir.

muhammad-ii-of-khwarazm.name: Muhammad II of Khwarazm
muhammad-ii-of-khwarazm.summary: Shah of the Khwarazmian Empire from 1200 to 1220, who expanded it to its greatest extent by 1218 before it was destroyed following a skirmish with the Mongols.

jebe.name: Jebe
jebe.summary: A prominent Mongol general under Genghis Khan (died c. 1224), originally an enemy soldier who became one of his greatest commanders and helped expand the Mongol Empire.

subutai.name: Subutai
subutai.summary: Mongol general (c. 1175–1248) and chief military strategist for Genghis Khan and Ögedei Khan, who directed over 20 campaigns and conquered more territory than any other commander in history.

abu-sa-id-bahadur-khan.name: Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan
abu-sa-id-bahadur-khan.summary: Ninth ruler of the Ilkhanate, the Mongol-founded state covering present-day Iran and neighboring lands, from about 1316 until his death in 1335, after which the Ilkhanate broke apart.

buyid-dynasty.name: Buyid dynasty
buyid-dynasty.summary: A Shia Muslim dynasty of Iranian Daylamite origin that ruled Iraq and central and southern Iran from 934 to 1062, reviving symbols of the Sasanian Empire.

majd-al-dawla.name: Majd al-Dawla
majd-al-dawla.summary: Last Buyid ruler of Ray, from 997 to 1029, a weak figurehead for most of his reign who was deposed by Mahmud of Ghazna.

ulugh-beg.name: Ulugh Beg
ulugh-beg.summary: A Timurid ruler (1394–1449), astronomer, and mathematician who built the renowned Ulugh Beg Observatory in Samarkand during the Timurid Renaissance, before being executed after his son's revolt.

abdal-latif-mirza.name: Abdal-Latif Mirza
abdal-latif-mirza.summary: Great-grandson of Timur and third son of Timurid ruler Ulugh Beg, living from about 1420 to 1450.

abu-sa-id-mirza.name: Abu Sa'id Mirza
abu-sa-id-mirza.summary: Ruler of the Timurid Empire (1424-1469) who reunified much of it after decades of civil war and was Babur's paternal grandfather; he was killed invading western Iran.

arpa-ke-un.name: Arpa Ke'un
arpa-ke-un.summary: Ilkhan who ruled the Mongol-founded Ilkhanate in Persia from 1335 to 1336, during its disintegration.

ariq-b-ke.name: Ariq Böke
ariq-b-ke.summary: Youngest son of Tolui and grandson of Genghis Khan, who claimed the Mongol throne after Möngke's death, sparking a civil war with his brother Kublai Khan.

uzun-hasan.name: Uzun Hasan
uzun-hasan.summary: The strongest ruler of the Turkoman Aq Qoyunlu state (r. 1452–1478), who defeated rival powers to build an empire spanning Iran, Iraq, and Anatolia.

sultan-husayn-bayqara.name: Husayn Bayqara
sultan-husayn-bayqara.summary: Timurid ruler of Herat from 1469 to 1506, celebrated as a great patron of the arts and learning during what's called the second Timurid Renaissance.

peripatetic-school.name: Peripatetic school
peripatetic-school.summary: A philosophical school founded by Aristotle in Athens in 335 BC, continuing his teachings on virtue and moderation after his death and reviving under Rome.

malik-shah-i.name: Malik-Shah I
malik-shah-i.summary: Third sultan of the Seljuk Empire from 1072 to 1092, under whom the empire reached its peak, though real power lay with his vizier Nizam al-Mulk.

nizam-al-mulk.name: Nizam al-Mulk
nizam-al-mulk.summary: Persian scholar and vizier of the Seljuk Empire (1018-1092) who became its de facto ruler for 20 years and founded a network of madrasas called the Nizamiyyas.

the-book-of-healing.name: The Book of Healing
the-book-of-healing.summary: A four-part scientific and philosophical encyclopedia by Avicenna, written around 1014–1027, covering logic, natural science, mathematics and metaphysics, meant to "heal" ignorance of the soul rather than treat the body.

kalam.name: Kalam
kalam.summary: The scholastic, rational study of Islamic theology, developed to defend Islamic beliefs against philosophical doubters, which rose to prominence under schools such as the Mu'tazilites, Ash'aris and Maturidis.

avicennism.name: Avicennism
avicennism.summary: A school of Islamic philosophy founded by Avicenna, based on his study of Aristotle, which became the dominant school of Islamic philosophy by the 12th century.

al-ghazali.name: Al-Ghazali
al-ghazali.summary: A Persian Sunni Muslim scholar and polymath (c. 1058-1111), regarded as one of Islamic history's most influential theologians, jurists and mystics.

qiyas.name: Qiyas
qiyas.summary: Process of deductive analogy in Islamic jurisprudence that applies known Quranic and hadith rulings to new situations, accepted by Sunni Muslims as a secondary source of Sharia law.

ibn-hazm.name: Ibn Hazm
ibn-hazm.summary: An Andalusian polymath, jurist and theologian (994–1064) from Córdoba, a leading codifier of the Zahiri legal school and one of the era's foremost thinkers.

shams-al-dawla.name: Shams al-Dawla
shams-al-dawla.summary: The Buyid ruler of Hamadan from 997 to 1021, son of Fakhr al-Dawla.

sama-al-dawla.name: Sama' al-Dawla
sama-al-dawla.summary: The Buyid ruler of Hamadan from 1021 to about 1023, son of Shams al-Dawla, whose short reign ended when a rival Kakuyid ruler overran the province.

ala-al-dawla-muhammad.name: Ala al-Dawla Muhammad
ala-al-dawla-muhammad.summary: A Daylamite military commander who founded the Kakuyid dynasty in 1008, ruling western Persia and Jibal until his death in 1041.

kakuyids.name: Kakuyids
kakuyids.summary: A Shia Muslim dynasty of Daylamite origin that ruled western Persia, Jibal and Kurdistan from about 1008 to 1051, later governing Isfahan and Yazd as atabegs until 1141.

gorgan.name: Gorgan
gorgan.summary: City in northern Iran near the Caspian Sea, capital of Golestan province, historically also known as Astarabad.

abu-ubayd-al-juzjani.name: Abu 'Ubayd al-Juzjani
abu-ubayd-al-juzjani.summary: Muslim physician and chronicler (d. 1070) who became Avicenna's pupil and lifelong companion, later completing Avicenna's autobiography after his death.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.name: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Iranian-American philosopher and Islamic scholar born in 1933, who taught philosophy in Tehran before the 1979 Islamic Revolution forced him into exile in the United States.

safavid-iran.name: Safavid Empire
safavid-iran.summary: One of the largest and longest-lasting Iranian empires, ruled by the Safavid dynasty from 1501 to 1736; Shah Ismail I made Twelver Shi'ism the state religion, a major turning point in Islamic history.

abbasid-caliphate.name: Abbasid Caliphate
abbasid-caliphate.summary: The third Islamic caliphate, ruling from 750 to 1258 with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time, known for ushering in the Islamic Golden Age of science and culture.

yarsanism.name: Yarsanism
yarsanism.summary: A syncretic monotheistic religion founded by Sultan Sahak in western Iran in the late 14th century, whose god manifests in one primary form and six secondary ones, together called the Holy Seven.

nizari-isma-ilism.name: Nizari Isma'ilism
nizari-isma-ilism.summary: The largest branch of the Ismailis, the second-largest branch of Shia Islam, whose spiritual leader today is the Aga Khan.

hasan-i-sabbah.name: Hasan-i Sabbah
hasan-i-sabbah.summary: Founder of the Nizari Ismaili sect and the Order of Assassins, who ruled the Nizari Ismaili state from the fortress of Alamut from 1090 to his death in 1124.

alamut-castle.name: Alamut Castle
alamut-castle.summary: Ruined mountain fortress in Iran that served as headquarters of the Nizari Ismaili state from 1090 until captured by the Mongols in 1256, famed for its gardens, library and laboratories.

daylam.name: Daylaman
daylam.summary: A mountainous inland region of Gilan, Iran, home to the Daylamites and the origin point of the Buyid dynasty around 930.

zaydism.name: Zaydism
zaydism.summary: A denomination of Shia Islam, also called Fiver Shia, that arose in the eighth century after Zayd ibn Ali's failed rebellion against the Umayyad Caliphate; most followers today live in Yemen.
